html:
"N. European Bronze Age cultures" is the map's label for northern Europe in 1500, 1000 and 700 BCE, the time archaeologists call the Nordic Bronze Age, about 1700 to 500 BCE, in Denmark, southern Sweden and Norway and northern Germany.

The north had no copper or tin of its own. It got bronze through long-distance trade and paid largely with amber from the Baltic and North Sea shores. Local smiths made it into weapons, jewellery and ritual objects of high skill, such as the curved horns called lurs and the Trundholm sun chariot, a horse pulling a gilded sun disc.

Chiefs were buried under great earth mounds, some in oak coffins that preserved their clothes. The Egtved Girl, buried in Denmark around 1370 BCE, still wore her woollen string skirt. Thousands of rock carvings, as at Tanum in Sweden, show ships, sun symbols, weapons and processions.

Further south lay the Urnfield cultures. As the climate cooled and iron spread, the Nordic Bronze Age gave way to the Pre-Roman Iron Age and the Jastorf culture, often linked with the early Germanic peoples.
